title: Denial of Service
description: Techniques aimed at degrading availability, exhausting hardware resources, stalling worker threads, and consuming connection limits.

attacks.name: HTTP flood
attacks.desc: Flooding web servers with a massive volume of legitimate-looking HTTP GET or POST requests to exhaust bandwidth, CPU, and web server worker threads.
attacks.prevention: Use edge rate limits, autoscaling, caching, and upstream DDoS protection for traffic floods.

attacks.name: Slowloris
attacks.desc: Opening hundreds of HTTP connections and transmitting partial headers at slow intervals (every few seconds), exhausting web server concurrent connection pools.
attacks.prevention: Set connection and header-read timeouts, per-client limits, and a cap on incomplete requests.

attacks.name: RUDY
attacks.desc: Sending HTTP POST requests with a large Content-Length header and transmitting body data at an extremely slow rate (e.g. 1 byte every 10 seconds) to tie up server threads.
attacks.prevention: Limit slow request bodies with read timeouts and minimum throughput requirements.

attacks.name: Hash collision DoS
attacks.desc: Submitting POST requests containing thousands of parameter keys engineered to produce identical hash table keys, degrading dictionary lookups from O(1) to O(n^2) CPU overhead.
attacks.prevention: Use maintained runtime hashing and impose limits on attacker-controlled collection sizes.

attacks.name: Regex DoS
attacks.desc: Transmitting crafted payloads into regular expressions that trigger catastrophic backtracking, locking CPU threads at 100% utilization for hours.
attacks.prevention: Use bounded, safe regular expressions and reject inputs that exceed expected size or complexity.

attacks.name: XML bomb
attacks.desc: Submitting small XML payloads containing recursively expanding entity definitions that expand into gigabytes in memory, crashing the XML parser process.

attacks.name: Large file upload
attacks.desc: Submitting oversized file uploads to endpoints lacking request body size limits, filling temporary disk partitions and exhausting network interface bandwidth.

attacks.name: Zip bomb
attacks.desc: Uploading small, highly compressed archives (e.g. a few kilobytes) that expand into gigabytes or terabytes during extraction, exhausting available disk space.

attacks.name: Decompression bomb
attacks.desc: Sending HTTP requests or files encoded with nested compression streams (gzip/bzip2) that overwhelm decompression routines with astronomical memory demands.

attacks.name: GraphQL complexity attack
attacks.desc: Crafting GraphQL queries requesting deeply nested relationships or computationally expensive fields across hundreds of aliases to overwhelm backend database pools.

attacks.name: Algorithmic complexity
attacks.desc: Supplying worst-case input configurations to internal algorithms (such as QuickSort with adversarial pivot inputs) to degrade execution from O(n log n) to O(n^2).

attacks.name: Memory exhaustion
attacks.desc: Triggering application endpoints that allocate unbounded buffers in memory without releasing references, driving the runtime into OutOfMemoryError crashes.

attacks.name: Connection pool exhaustion
attacks.desc: Opening slow or unclosed transactions that hold open database connection pool slots, preventing legitimate application threads from communicating with datastores.

attacks.name: Session table exhaustion
attacks.desc: Automating millions of unauthenticated initial requests to flood in-memory session stores (Redis, Memcached), triggering evictions and crashing session managers.
